pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- List some types of manure used by farmers.
- Identify and write down the materials used in preparing manure and their sources.
- Categorise manure into those from plant wastes and animal wastes.
- Compile a list of plant parts and wastes, and animal parts and wastes, that are used to prepare manure.
- Justify the use of different animal and plant manures under different soil and climatic conditions.

pages.title: What is Manure?
pages.body: Manure is organic material, derived from plant or animal waste, that is added to soil to improve its fertility and structure, supplying nutrients that support healthy crop growth. Manure differs from manufactured chemical fertiliser in that it comes from natural, organic sources, and it generally also improves soil structure over time, helping soil retain water and support beneficial soil organisms, in addition to supplying nutrients.

questions.q: Manure is best described as
o: Organic material from plant or animal waste added to improve soil
questions.e: Manure is organic material, derived from plant or animal waste, that is added to soil to improve its fertility and structure, supplying nutrients that support healthy crop growth.

pages.title: Manure from Animal Waste
pages.body:
Poultry droppings, cow dung, pig dung, human excreta, and animal parts or carcases are common sources of manure derived from animal waste, and this lesson treats each individually, since they differ in nutrient content and how they should be handled.

- Poultry droppings are a particularly nutrient rich manure, high in nitrogen and phosphorus, produced from chickens, guinea fowl and other domestic birds, and are commonly collected from poultry housing for use on farms.

- Cow dung is a widely available manure in farming communities that keep cattle, moderate in nutrient content but valuable for improving soil structure due to its high fibre content from the cow's largely plant based diet.

- Pig dung is another commonly available animal manure, generally rich in nitrogen, sourced from pig housing on farms that keep pigs.

- Human excreta, properly treated and composted to eliminate disease causing organisms, has historically been used as a manure source in some farming systems, though it requires particularly careful handling to avoid spreading disease.

- Animal parts and carcases, such as bones, blood and other slaughterhouse waste, can be processed into nutrient rich manure, particularly valuable for supplying phosphorus and other minerals, though they require careful composting to avoid attracting pests or spreading disease.

pages.title: Manure from Plant Waste
pages.body:
Leaves, waste fruits, other plant parts and shavings, and domestic refuse containing plant material are common sources of manure derived from plant waste, each contributing differently to the finished manure.

- Leaves, particularly fallen leaves collected from trees and shrubs, break down into a manure that is generally moderate in nutrients but excellent for improving soil texture and water retention.

- Waste fruits and vegetable trimmings, often available from markets, households or food processing, decompose relatively quickly and contribute useful nutrients, particularly potassium, to the finished manure.

- Other plant parts and shavings, such as sawdust, wood shavings, and crop residues like maize stalks or rice husks, add bulk and fibre to manure, though they generally decompose more slowly than softer plant material and can temporarily reduce available soil nitrogen while they break down.

- Domestic refuse containing plant material, such as vegetable peelings and food scraps from households, can also be composted into manure, provided non organic waste such as plastic is carefully removed first.

[[pic:A two column labelled chart, one column headed Animal Waste Manure showing small icons for poultry droppings, cow dung, pig dung and animal parts, and the other column headed Plant Waste Manure showing small icons for fallen leaves, waste fruit, crop residues and wood shavings, with a simple arrow from both columns pointing to a single labelled compost heap.]]

Notice how manure sources fall naturally into these two broad categories, based on whether they originate from animals or from plants, even though both categories are ultimately combined and treated in similar ways, as explored further in the next lesson, to produce finished manure suitable for improving soil.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Justifying Manure Choice Under Different Soil and Climatic Conditions

pages.title: Justifying Manure Choice Under Different Soil and Climatic Conditions
pages.body: The choice of which manure to use, and how much, often depends on the specific soil type and climate of a particular farming area. Sandy soils, which drain quickly and hold few nutrients, benefit particularly from manures that improve water retention and add organic bulk, such as decomposed leaves or crop residues, alongside nutrient rich manures like poultry droppings to compensate for the soil's naturally low fertility. Clay soils, which can become compacted and poorly aerated, benefit from manures that improve soil structure and drainage, again favouring fibrous plant based manures such as cow dung. In areas with a long dry season, slower decomposing manures such as wood shavings or crop residues can provide a more gradual, longer lasting nutrient release, while in areas with heavier, more consistent rainfall, faster decomposing, nutrient rich manures such as poultry droppings may be replenished more frequently to match nutrient loss through leaching.

pages.title: Types of Manure and Where Each is Best Used
pages.body:
| **MANURE** | **SOURCE** | **QUALITIES** | **BEST USE** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Poultry droppings** | Chickens and other birds | The richest common manure in nitrogen and phosphorus. Fresh droppings can burn crops, so they are first cured | Vegetables and maize, in small amounts |
| **Cow dung** | Cattle | Bulky, with lower amounts of nutrients. It greatly improves soil structure | Sandy soils, to help them hold water |
| **Pig dung** | Pigs | Wet and fairly rich. It must be well rotted | Heavy feeders such as maize and plantain |
| **Sheep and goat droppings** | Sheep and goats | Dry pellets that are richer than cow dung and easy to carry | Vegetable beds |
| **Human excreta** | People | Rich in nutrients but may carry germs and worms. It must be fully composted for many months | Tree crops, never vegetables that are eaten raw |
| **Animal parts and carcases** | Bones, blood, horns and dead animals | Bone meal is rich in phosphorus and calcium, and blood meal in nitrogen | Tree crops and root crops |
| **Compost** | Leaves, waste fruits, plant parts, domestic refuse and shavings rotted in a heap or pit | Balanced, safe and rich in humus | All soils and all crops |
| **Green manure** | A quick growing legume such as mucuna or cowpea that is ploughed into the soil at flowering | Adds nitrogen and humus where the crop is to be grown | Poor soils before the main crop |
| **Farmyard manure** | A mixture of animal droppings, urine and bedding from animal houses | Rich in nitrogen and potassium when well rotted | Most field crops |

Soil and climate guide the choice of manure. Sandy soils lose water and nutrients quickly, so they need bulky manures such as cow dung and compost. Clay soils are heavy, so they need coarse compost that opens the soil. In areas of heavy rain, well rotted manure is applied in small amounts at intervals, because nutrients are easily washed away. In dry areas manure is covered or worked into the soil so that it does not dry out and lose nitrogen to the air.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Combining different manure sources, such as mixing a nitrogen rich animal manure with a fibre rich plant based manure, often produces better results than relying on a single source alone, since this combination can supply a more balanced mix of nutrients while also improving soil structure. Many experienced farmers develop their own preferred manure combinations based on years of observing what works best for their particular soil and local climate.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Prepare manure from the different plant and animal wastes.
- Discuss the preparation of manure using the plants and animal wastes that are available in a community.

pages.title: From Raw Waste to Finished Manure
pages.body: Raw plant and animal waste, as described in Lesson 7, is not always immediately safe or ready to apply directly to soil, since fresh waste can contain disease causing organisms, weed seeds, or substances that could harm young plants if used incorrectly. Preparing manure properly, through composting or curing, transforms raw waste into a safer, more effective soil improver.

pages.title: Composting
pages.body: Composting is a method of preparing manure in which plant and animal waste is piled together and allowed to decompose under controlled conditions, with the help of naturally occurring bacteria, fungi and other decomposer organisms. A well made compost heap generally layers different materials, alternating nitrogen rich materials, such as fresh animal manure or kitchen waste, with carbon rich materials, such as dry leaves or straw, since this balance helps decomposer organisms break down the waste efficiently. The heap is kept moist, but not waterlogged, and is turned periodically to supply oxygen to the decomposing organisms, speeding up the process and helping control unpleasant odours.

pages.title: Curing
pages.body:
Curing refers to allowing prepared manure to rest for a further period after the most active stage of decomposition has slowed, allowing the material to stabilise fully, cool down, and lose any remaining harmful organisms or excess ammonia that could otherwise damage young plants if applied too soon. Manure that has not been properly cured can sometimes be too strong or too hot, in terms of its ongoing chemical activity, for direct use around sensitive seedlings.

[[pic:A cutaway diagram of a compost heap showing alternating layers, labelled from bottom to top, coarse plant material for drainage, animal manure, dry leaves, kitchen waste, and a final covering layer of soil or straw, with a small thermometer icon inserted into the heap and an arrow showing turning with a fork.]]

Notice how the layered structure of a compost heap combines both animal and plant waste sources studied in Lesson 7, and how turning and moisture control are shown as ongoing tasks throughout the composting process, not one time actions.

pages.title: General Steps in Preparing Manure
pages.body:
Collecting and sorting waste, layering or mixing materials, maintaining suitable moisture and aeration, and allowing sufficient time for decomposition and curing are four general steps that apply across most manure preparation methods, whether the specific waste used is animal or plant based.

- Collecting and sorting waste involves gathering available plant and animal waste materials and removing any non organic contamination, such as plastic or metal, before use.

- Layering or mixing materials involves combining nitrogen rich and carbon rich waste in reasonable proportions, since a mixture generally decomposes more effectively than any single material alone.

- Maintaining suitable moisture and aeration involves watering the heap if it becomes too dry, and turning it periodically to allow air to reach the decomposing material throughout, since decomposition slows considerably without enough oxygen.

- Allowing sufficient time for decomposition and curing involves waiting, generally several weeks to a few months depending on the materials and conditions, until the manure has broken down into a dark, crumbly, earthy smelling material, safe and ready for use on crops.

pages.title: Adapting Preparation to Locally Available Waste
pages.body: Since the specific plant and animal waste available differs from one community to another, depending on local farming and livestock practices, preparing manure often means adapting the general method to whatever materials are realistically at hand. A community with many poultry farms might build compost heaps centred around poultry droppings mixed with available crop residues, while a community with more cattle rearing might centre their compost around cow dung mixed with grass or leaves. Discussing and comparing these local variations helps farmers learn from each other and adapt manure preparation to their own specific circumstances, rather than relying on a single, rigid method that may not suit every situation.

lessons.title: Conditions for Good Compost and a Comparison of the Heap and Pit Methods

pages.title: Conditions for Good Compost and a Comparison of the Heap and Pit Methods
pages.body:
| **CONDITION** | **WHAT IS NEEDED** | **REASON** |
|---|---|---|
| **Materials** | A mixture of green materials such as fresh leaves, vegetable waste and animal droppings, and brown materials such as dry leaves, straw and wood shavings | Green materials supply nitrogen and brown materials supply carbon. Microorganisms need both |
| **Moisture** | Damp like a squeezed sponge | Microorganisms cannot work in a dry heap, and a soaked heap has no air |
| **Air** | Turn the heap every two to three weeks | The useful microorganisms need oxygen. Without it the heap smells bad and rots slowly |
| **Heat** | The centre of a good heap becomes hot, up to about 60 degrees Celsius | The heat shows that microorganisms are active, and it kills many weed seeds and germs |
| **Time** | About two to three months | Finished compost is dark, crumbly and smells like soil |

| **FEATURE** | **HEAP METHOD** | **PIT METHOD** |
|---|---|---|
| **Position** | Above the ground | In a pit about one metre deep |
| **Best season and place** | The rainy season and wet areas, because it drains well | The dry season and dry areas, because it keeps moisture |
| **Turning** | Easy | Harder |
| **Problem to avoid** | Drying out, so it is covered with grass or palm fronds | Waterlogging when it rains |

pages.title: From Knowledge to Hands On Practice
pages.body: Lessons 7 and 8 built up the knowledge needed to identify manure sources and understand the general methods used to prepare manure. This final lesson in the strand focuses on actually carrying out manure preparation practically, in the field or school garden, turning that knowledge into a genuine, hands on farming skill.

questions.q: Which of the following best summarises the purpose of this lesson?
o: Ignoring all knowledge from previous lessons
Memorising manure sources with no practical activity
Studying manure preparation only in theory with no practical component
Turning knowledge of manure sources and preparation methods into hands on practice
questions.e: From Knowledge to Hands On Practice Lessons 7 and 8 built up the knowledge needed to identify manure sources and understand the general methods used to prepare manure.

pages.title: Cleaning and Sorting Waste
pages.body: Cleaning and sorting is the first practical stage of manure preparation, involving collecting available plant and animal waste and carefully removing any non organic material, such as plastic bags, glass or metal, that would not decompose and could contaminate the finished manure. Sorting also involves separating waste broadly into nitrogen rich materials, such as fresh manure or kitchen scraps, and carbon rich materials, such as dry leaves or crop residues, ready for the layering stage that follows.

pages.title: Building the Compost Heap or Pit
pages.body:
Once waste has been cleaned and sorted, it is built up into a compost heap or placed into a compost pit, typically alternating layers of nitrogen rich and carbon rich material, as described in Lesson 8. A layer of soil is often added between other layers, and a thin covering of soil, straw or leaves is placed over the very top, helping to retain moisture and control odour. Choosing a level, well drained site, ideally partly shaded to prevent the heap from drying out too quickly in strong sun, helps the composting process proceed smoothly.

[[pic:A step by step photographic style sequence showing four stages of practical compost making in a school garden, first learners sorting collected plant and animal waste into two piles, then learners layering the sorted waste into a compost heap, then a learner watering the heap lightly, and finally a learner turning the heap with a fork several weeks later, with the resulting dark, crumbly compost visible.]]

Notice how each stage shown reflects the general steps studied in Lesson 8, sorting, layering, maintaining moisture, and turning, now applied as an actual, practical activity that could be carried out in a school garden or community farm.

pages.title: Monitoring, Turning and Curing
pages.body: Once a compost heap or pit has been built, it needs regular attention over several weeks or months. Checking moisture levels and adding water if the heap feels dry, turning the material periodically to supply oxygen and encourage even decomposition, and watching for a change in appearance, smell and texture are all part of monitoring the compost as it develops. Once decomposition has clearly slowed and the material has become dark and crumbly, allowing a further curing period, without turning, lets the manure stabilise fully before it is used on crops.

pages.title: Safety and Good Practice
pages.body: Wearing gloves when handling raw animal waste, washing hands thoroughly afterwards, and avoiding direct contact between raw, uncomposted waste and food crops are important safety practices when preparing manure practically. These precautions help prevent the spread of disease causing organisms that may be present in fresh animal waste or human excreta before the composting and curing process has had time to reduce them to safe levels.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Schools that maintain an ongoing composting area in their garden give learners repeated, real opportunities to practise every stage of manure preparation across a full term or year, from collecting waste to eventually applying finished manure to school crops, providing a complete, practical understanding of the process that complements the knowledge built up in Lessons 7 and 8.
